title: Almost (Acts 26)
hookLine: King Agrippa says almost thou persuadest me

lines: A KING ARRIVES WITH GREAT POMP.
A PRISONER IN A HALL OF POWER.
cards: Two years pass. Paul sits in custody in Caesarea, on the coast, while governors come and go.
Then a new governor, Festus, gets a royal visit: King Agrippa and Bernice arrive with great pomp, the text says, with commanders and the city's leading men.
Festus has a prisoner he doesn't know what to do with, and the king is curious. So Paul is brought in, in chains, to a hall full of power, and invited to speak.

teach.h: HARD TO KICK AGAINST THE GOAD.
teach.b: Paul tells it again: the road, the light at midday brighter than the sun, the voice. This time he includes a line he hasn't mentioned before.
The voice said, in the Douay-Rheims, "It is hard for thee to kick against the goad," like an ox kicking the stick that steers it. Paul had been fighting what was pulling him.
He tells how he was sent to open eyes and turn people from darkness to light. Festus can't take it.
He shouts: "Paul, thou art beside thyself: much learning doth make thee mad." Paul answers calmly, I am not mad, most noble Festus. Then he turns to the king.
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do.

teach.h: IN A LITTLE THOU PERSUADEST ME.
teach.b: And Agrippa replies, in the Douay-Rheims: "In a little thou persuadest me to become a Christian." The King James turns that into almost, today's word. And there's Antioch's word, Christian, in a king's mouth.
What did Agrippa mean? Honestly, nobody's sure. The Greek is two short words, en oligo, in a little.
It could mean almost, or in such a short time, or with so little effort. He might be moved; he might be brushing Paul off with a smile.
Paul's answer works either way: I would to God that, in a little and in much, not only you but all who hear me today might become such as I am, "except these bands."

teach.h: IN A LITTLE, AND IN MUCH.
teach.b: Picture him raising his chained hands. Then the king rises, and the hearing is over. This man could have gone free, Agrippa remarks, if he hadn't appealed to Caesar.

how: Catholics are encouraged to examine their consciences regularly, often at night, noticing what they have left undone as well as done, and many bring those things to the sacrament of reconciliation.

s: we know Agrippa was nearly converted

Paul tells his story to Agrippa with a line he left out in Jerusalem
before the king, he adds: it is hard for thee to kick against the goad.
Festus thought Paul had lost his mind
he shouted that much learning had made him mad.

games.q: you're Paul. the king has just said, in a little thou persuadest me. what do you say?
o: press him hard to decide now.
wish everyone listening were like you, except the chains.
thank him and say nothing more.
games.why: he wishes that all who hear him, in a little and in much, might become such as he is, except these bands. then the king rises and the hearing ends.

practice: Think of one thing you've almost done for a long time: almost called, almost forgiven, almost started, almost gone to confession, or to Mass, or to the doctor.

Name it quietly and notice what has kept it at almost, fear, pride, the schedule, a little embarrassment, then picture just the next small step that would move it from almost to altogether. If you pray, offer that one step.

wordCard.voice: Almost. King Agrippa's answer to Paul, maybe moved, maybe joking, and Paul's wish that all who heard him might become as he was. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: in a little. Agrippa's two words, which may mean almost, in so short a time, or with so little effort.
